homelessness.explainer: "Housing First" means giving someone a permanent place to live right away, without first requiring them to get sober or accept treatment — the idea is that it's easier to deal with addiction or mental illness once you have a roof over your head. A "conservatorship" is a court order that puts another person or agency in charge of decisions for someone a judge finds unable to care for themselves. "CARE Court" is a newer civil court track that can order a treatment plan for people with serious untreated mental illness. The "point-in-time count" (PIT count) is a one-night tally each January of how many people are homeless.
homelessness.current_policy: California's official rule is "Housing First": state-funded programs are supposed to offer people permanent housing right away, without first requiring them to get sober or accept treatment. This is written into state law (Welfare & Institutions Code §8255). On top of that, the state has recently added enforcement and treatment options. The CARE Act ([SB 1338](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220SB1338), passed in 2022) set up civil courts that can order a treatment plan for people with untreated schizophrenia-type disorders, and every county was running it by December 2024. [Proposition 1](https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2024/prop-1-mental-health/) (March 2024) approved a $6.4 billion bond for mental-health housing and treatment and shifted some existing mental-health funds. After the U.S. Supreme Court's [Grants Pass v. Johnson](https://calmatters.org/housing/2024/06/california-homeless-camps-grants-pass-ruling/) ruling (June 2024), Governor Newsom told state agencies and cities to clear encampments and shared a model anti-camping ordinance they could adopt.
key_facts: 187,084 Californians were counted as homeless in the January 2024 one-night count, up 3.1% from 181,399 the year before (HUD).
California has roughly 25% of the nation's homeless population and the highest share living outside — about two-thirds sleep on the street rather than in shelters.

[Grants Pass v. Johnson](https://calmatters.org/housing/2024/06/california-homeless-camps-grants-pass-ruling/) (Supreme Court, 6-3, June 2024) ruled that banning public camping does not violate the Eighth Amendment. That removed the earlier legal barrier to ticketing or arresting people for camping even when no shelter is available.

[Proposition 1](https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2024/prop-1-mental-health/) (2024) approved $6.4 billion for mental-health housing and treatment, including about $4.4 billion to build roughly 10,000 treatment beds.

By early 2026, more than 3,800 CARE Act petitions had been filed since the program went statewide in December 2024, and the state added $291 million in March 2026 for CARE-related services and housing.
homelessness.comparison: California's 3% increase in 2024 was much smaller than the roughly 18% jump nationwide. But the state still has the most homeless people of any state, the largest share of the country's total, and the highest portion sleeping outside. Most other big states get a far larger share of their homeless residents into shelters.
homelessness.arguments_for_change: People who favor a services-led, Housing First approach (the high end of the scale) say a stable home is what makes it possible to tackle addiction and mental illness — not a reward you earn afterward. They point to studies showing Housing First keeps people housed. They argue that clearing camps just moves people around without shrinking the population, and saddles them with criminal records that make it even harder to find housing. And they warn that expanding forced treatment or conservatorship risks coercing people who were never offered enough voluntary help first.
homelessness.arguments_against_change: People who favor more enforcement, treatment mandates, and conservatorship (the low end) say California has spent over $20 billion on homelessness in recent years while the share living outside stayed near the highest in the country. They argue that housing alone doesn't work for the many people on the street with untreated serious mental illness or addiction, that visible encampments create real health and safety problems, and that the Grants Pass ruling now lets the state pair an offer of shelter and treatment with consequences if someone refuses.

healthcare_funding.explainer: "Single-payer" means one government plan pays everyone's medical bills, instead of many private insurance companies. The "ACA" (Affordable Care Act, also called Obamacare) is the federal law that created subsidized marketplaces where people can buy coverage. "Medi-Cal" is California's version of Medicaid — the public health coverage program for low-income residents.
healthcare_funding.current_policy: California uses a mix of private insurance plus heavy government help, rather than one state-run plan. Covered California is the state's Affordable Care Act (ACA) marketplace, where people buy coverage, and the state chips in to lower premiums. Medi-Cal — California's version of Medicaid, the public coverage program for low-income residents — was expanded on January 1, 2024 to cover all eligible undocumented adults, making California the first state to offer full Medicaid coverage no matter someone's immigration status. Efforts to switch to a single government-run plan have repeatedly failed: [AB 1400](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220AB1400) (the CalCare bill, 2022) was withdrawn before a vote, and its follow-up, [AB 2200](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240AB2200) (2024), was stopped in committee.
key_facts: Medi-Cal extended full coverage to all eligible adults regardless of immigration status on January 1, 2024 — the first state to do so.

[AB 1400](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220AB1400) (CalCare) died on January 31, 2022 when its author pulled it, short of the 41 Assembly votes it needed. Its 2024 follow-up, [AB 2200](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240AB2200), was held up in the Appropriations committee.
Analysts estimated CalCare would cost roughly $314–391 billion a year — more than the state's entire general-fund budget — and would require new payroll, business, and high-income taxes.

A single-payer plan would need the federal government to sign off (through what are called Section 1332 and Medicaid/Medicare waivers) to redirect federal money. A federal law called ERISA also limits how much a state can regulate the self-funded health plans that many large employers use.
California's uninsured rate dropped to about 6–7% in recent years — among the lowest ever — thanks to ACA subsidies and the Medi-Cal expansion, not a single-payer system.
healthcare_funding.comparison: No U.S. state runs a single-payer system. Vermont passed one in 2014, then dropped it because it couldn't figure out how to pay for it. California chose a different path — expanding subsidies and Medicaid — and got to one of the lowest uninsured rates in the country while keeping the private insurance market in place.
healthcare_funding.arguments_for_change: People who want to move toward a state single-payer plan (the high end) say one public plan would cut out insurance-company overhead, premiums, deductibles, and limited provider networks. They point to some analyses (such as a UC Berkeley Labor Center estimate) that projected the whole system could spend less overall. They argue that covering everyone — regardless of job or immigration status — is simpler to run, and that California's sheer size would give it leverage to negotiate lower prices.
healthcare_funding.arguments_against_change: People who want to keep the current subsidized private market (the low end) say single-payer's roughly $300–400 billion-a-year price tag would mean steep new taxes, with no guarantee of net savings. They note it depends on federal sign-offs and ERISA exceptions that might never come. They warn that upending the employer and Medicare coverage most people already have is risky, both politically and practically — and that California already reached near-universal coverage by expanding subsidies and Medi-Cal without that upheaval.

abortion.current_policy: Abortion is a right written into California's constitution. [Proposition 1](https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2022) (November 2022), approved by about 66% of voters, amended the state constitution to bar California from denying or interfering with reproductive freedom, including abortion and contraception. After the U.S. Supreme Court's 2022 Dobbs decision ended the federal right to abortion, the Legislature passed a set of laws. [AB 1242](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220AB1242) and [AB 2091](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220AB2091) (2022) stop California police, businesses, and providers from helping with out-of-state abortion investigations or handing over related records. [SB 345](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SB345) (2023) protects California-licensed providers — including those offering telehealth and abortion pills — from being prosecuted or extradited by other states. Medi-Cal covers abortion at full state cost, and the state has set aside more than $200 million to support abortion access and providers.
key_facts: [Proposition 1](https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2022) (2022) passed with about 66% support, writing an explicit right to abortion and contraception into the state constitution.
Medi-Cal covers abortion with the state paying the full cost, and private insurance plans regulated by the state are generally required to cover it too.

California passed shield laws — [AB 1242](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220AB1242), [AB 2091](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220AB2091) (2022) and [SB 345](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SB345) (2023) — that protect in-state providers and patients (including out-of-state patients using telehealth) from being pulled into other states' abortion prosecutions.
The state has set aside more than $200 million across recent budgets to fund abortion access, expand provider capacity, and help patients with costs such as travel.
After Dobbs, California set itself up as a place patients from states with bans could travel to for care, with state funding to support them.
abortion.comparison: California is one of the most protective states for abortion access after Dobbs, pairing a constitutional right, Medi-Cal coverage, public funding, and provider shield laws. That stands in sharp contrast to the more than a dozen states that ban or sharply restrict abortion, and puts California in a small group of states that openly fund and protect care for patients coming from elsewhere.
abortion.arguments_for_change: People who want to expand protections further (the high end) say that as more states impose bans, California should act as a refuge — funding travel and care for out-of-state patients, broadening provider protections and capacity, and getting ahead of any future federal limits. They argue that cost and logistics, not just whether something is legal, decide whether people can actually get care, so the state should fund and shield it aggressively.
abortion.arguments_against_change: People who favor some limits, or simply not expanding further (the low end), argue on moral or religious grounds that abortion should face some restrictions, such as limits later in pregnancy. They say public money shouldn't pay for abortion or for out-of-state patients' care, and that shield laws and refuge funding drag California into fights with other states' laws and stretch what taxpayers are asked to cover. Within California, this is a minority view given Prop 1's 66% margin.
